newsitem.title: FRANCE: Central France heads for big barley, wheat crops.
newsitem.headline: Central France heads for big barley, wheat crops.

text.p: The central France grain belt is heading for large harvests of barley, wheat and rapeseed this year as the crops emerged largely unscathed from a prolonged drought in the spring, local crop analysts said on Friday.
But the size of the crop and harvest delays caused by wet weather would create logistical problems for farmers who must gather all the grains at the same time, they said.
"Overall this will be a satisfactory year for central France. We had some good surprises," an official for the statistics service of the ONIC grain office in Orleans said.
The winter barley harvest was due to start around June 20 but the rain pushed the starting date back to July 7. The soft wheat harvest got under way around July 11.
Harvesting was now 95 percent complete for winter barley, 70 percent for rapeseed, 15 percent for soft wheat and 5-10 percent for durum wheat.
A dry spell of nearly three months in the spring had raised fears that yields could be hit. But initial reports from the fields now suggested that rapeseed had made a strong recovery.
Barley and wheat in the rich soils of the Beauce area in north would be up sharply from last year.
But on the light soils of the south, rain in May and June came too late to help crops fully recover.
In the Eure et Loire area soft wheat yields might hit 6.7 tonnes per hectare and in the north some fields were reporting yields as high as 10 tonnes.
Overall the average yield for the region could reach 6.7 to 7.2 tonnes per hectare, against 6.4 tonnes last year and a record 6.9 in 1991. Last year's yields suffered from a prolonged spring drought.
"We have all the chances to beat the 1991 record," the official said.
Assuming a three percent rise in area, the region might harvest 15 to 20 percent more soft wheat than last year, he said.
But in the south, wet weather in June led to some unwanted germination in the fields and quality would be hit, though it was too early to assess the extent of the damage.
Protein content, a key measurement of milling wheat quality, was also expected to decline. "We will have some wheat that is not fit for milling," the analyst said.
The June rain did not hurt wheat crops in the north because they had not yet reached maturity.
But the return of wet conditions this week had revived fears over quality and possible harvest disruption.
Winter barley yields might reach a "satisfactory" six tonnes per hectare in the south against 6.5 tonnes last year. But the Beauce area was expected to report "exceptional" yields of 7-8 tonnes.
Overall the region's average barley yield could exceed last year's 6.0 tonnes. Assuming a 13.5 percent rise in area, this would provide for a 15-20 percent jump in output.
Initial results suggested barley quality was good, with a protein content of 10.5-11 percent, making it fit for malting. Specific weight was satisfactory and there were no germination problems.

Rapeseed yields were now seen rising to 3.5-4 tonnes from 3.46 last year. Assuming the area rose 28 percent to 176,000 hectares, this could lead to a 30-40 percent rise in output from the 470,000 tonnes harvested last year.
